subsection: 4. How the global economy is organised

notes.b: A basic processing unit is a factory carrying out one stage of production: processing a raw material, making a component (a part that goes into a finished product) or assembling a product. Multinational companies (MNCs, firms operating in many countries) place each stage in whichever country suits it best, which is why production is so widely spread.
points: The Intel and Apple chains, such as those in 'One multinational company (MNC)', are examples of stages spread across several countries.
Cheap labour suits labour-intensive assembly (work that needs many workers rather than machines), so firms put assembly where wages are low.
Units are placed close to raw materials or to markets, which cuts the distance inputs or finished goods must travel.
A factory inside a trade bloc (a group of countries with shared trade rules) sells to the bloc's members without the barriers that apply to imports from outside.
Tax breaks (reduced tax bills) and grants (money from government) lower the cost of operating in a country, so they attract factories.
Falling transport and communication costs make distant factories practical, because a plant far away can still be supplied and managed.
Spreading production across many countries means that one disaster or strike does not stop all production, so the firm spreads its risk.
notes.tip: If asked how basic processing units are spread worldwide, give the reasons for locating each stage in a different country and name an example such as Nike or Intel.

notes.b: Nike shows how far a firm can spread production: it designs and sells shoes but owns almost none of the factories that make them. Do not say Nike owns its Asian factories.
points: Founded as Blue Ribbon Sports in 1964 by Phil Knight and Bill Bowerman; renamed Nike in 1971.
Headquarters, design and marketing are in Beaverton, Oregon, USA, so the high-skill, high-value work stays at home.
Footwear is made by independent contract factories (outside firms paid to make the product), mainly in Vietnam (the largest), China and Indonesia.
Nike sells its products worldwide.

Sweatshop criticism in the 1990s (attacks on factories with very low pay and poor conditions), including of factories in Indonesia, led to factory monitoring and published supplier lists (lists of the factories Nike uses).
notes.tip: Nike is a 'manufacturer without factories'. Say it uses contract factories and do not say it owns its Asian factories.

notes.h: Export processing zones (EPZs) and Special Economic Zones
notes.b: Governments attract factories by creating special areas with easy trade rules. In an export processing zone, firms import components and export finished goods free of customs duty (a tax on goods crossing a border), and they receive tax breaks.
points: Shannon Free Zone, Co. Clare, set up in 1959, was one of the world's first export processing zones and Ireland's pioneer. The duty-free shop at Shannon Airport was 1947, so do not swap the dates.
Shenzhen, China, became a Special Economic Zone (a region with special business rules to attract foreign firms) in 1980.
Maquiladoras are assembly plants along Mexico's border with the USA, such as those at Tijuana and Ciudad Juárez, set up from 1965.
A maquiladora imports components duty-free and exports finished goods to the USA, so it is an example of an export processing zone at work.
notes.tip: Shannon Free Zone was 1959 and the duty-free shop was 1947. Do not swap them.

notes.b: Spreading production across many countries brings risks as well as savings. The costs fall on supply chains, workers and the environment.
points: Long supply chains (the linked stages from raw material to finished product) are vulnerable to disruption, as the 2021 chip shortage, the Ever Given blockage and the Red Sea diversions showed. There is more on this in 'Patterns in world trade'.
Branch plants (factories owned by a firm whose headquarters is elsewhere) close when costs change, and their workers lose jobs.
Some plants pay low wages and have poor conditions.
Moving components and goods over long distances has an environmental cost.
Responses include reshoring (moving production back to the home country) and friend-shoring (moving it to politically allied countries).

notes.b: At world scale, regions play different roles in the global economy. The core is the wealthy, powerful centre; the periphery is the poorer edge that supplies it.
points: Core regions have capital (money to invest), MNC headquarters, research and development, skilled labour, good infrastructure and political power.
The core's examples are the USA, western Europe's Blue Banana (Europe's core belt of dense development) and Japan.
The periphery supplies raw materials, food and cheap labour, with weak infrastructure and out-migration of people (people leaving to find work elsewhere).
Most of sub-Saharan Africa, parts of Latin America and parts of South Asia are periphery.

notes.b: Some countries sit between the core and the periphery. They are changing their role in the global economy.
points: The semi-periphery is made up of newly industrialised countries (NICs, countries that have recently built large manufacturing industries) moving towards the core.
South Korea did so earlier; China, India, Brazil and Mexico are doing so now.

notes.b: The core did not become rich by accident. An early start, overseas empires and a self-reinforcing cycle of growth built its lead.
points: Britain industrialised first, from the late 18th century (the Industrial Revolution), followed by western Europe and the USA.
Colonial empires supplied the core with raw materials and markets, and profits were reinvested in the core, which strengthened it further.
Cumulative causation, a model by Gunnar Myrdal (1957), says success attracts more investment, people and services, which increases success.
Backwash effects drain capital and skilled people from the periphery to the core, so the core grows at the periphery's expense.
The Blue Banana runs from south-east England and London through the Benelux countries and the Rhine valley to northern Italy. There is more on this in 'Socio-economic regions'.
notes.tip: If asked how core and peripheral regions developed, cover both: how the core grew (early industrialisation, empires, cumulative causation) and how the periphery fell behind.

notes.h: How the periphery developed, or failed to
notes.b: The periphery's economy was shaped by outside rulers for their benefit, which left it badly placed after independence.
points: Colonial economies were built around exporting one or two raw materials, so they had little other industry.
Railways ran from mines and plantations to ports, rather than linking regions to each other, because their purpose was export.
Borders were drawn by the colonisers, not by the people who lived there.
After independence these economies depended on falling commodity prices (the prices of raw materials), were burdened by debt and suffered conflict.

notes.b: Core and periphery are not fixed. Some places have moved up the ladder, and the North-South model is a simple picture of the pattern.
points: Spread effects (the benefits of growth passing outwards from the core) and investment can raise peripheral regions.
The Asian Tigers and China moved from periphery to semi-periphery or core in about two generations.
Ireland moved from the European periphery to a core-like economy through MNC investment. There is more on this in 'Irish Regions - Core and Peripheral'.
The Brandt Line, from the Brandt Report of 1980, is a simple North-South model (a line dividing richer northern from poorer southern countries) of the same pattern.
notes.tip: Criticism of the North-South idea is not needed here; it belongs to the Global Interdependence option.

notes.h: Sub-Saharan Africa: the main excluded region
notes.b: Sub-Saharan Africa is the main region excluded from world manufacturing. It has a very small share of world manufacturing and exports mostly unprocessed raw materials.
points: Nigeria: crude oil is most of its exports.
Zambia: copper is most of its exports.
The Democratic Republic of the Congo produces most of the world's cobalt and exports it raw despite its huge reserves, amid conflict.
Sudan: civil war between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces since April 2023 has caused one of the world's largest displacement crises, with people forced to flee their homes.
South Sudan became independent from Sudan in 2011, taking most of the oil fields.
The 2023 war is within Sudan, not a war with South Sudan, because they have been separate countries since 2011.
notes.tip: Say Africa's share of world manufacturing is 'very small' and give no percentage. Sudan and South Sudan are separate countries, so do not call the 2023 war a war with South Sudan. A short question may ask you to name an excluded region and give one reason.

notes.b: Many linked problems keep sub-Saharan Africa out of manufacturing. Each one raises costs or risks for firms, or limits what the countries can do for themselves.
points: Poor infrastructure: roads and ports are inadequate and electricity is unreliable, which makes running a factory costly.
Landlocked countries (with no coast): Africa has 16, such as Chad, Niger, Mali and South Sudan, and they face high transport costs to reach ports.
Political instability, conflict and corruption scare off investment.
Low levels of education and skills, and poor health, limit the workforce.
Small, poor home markets give firms little reason to produce locally.
Heavy debt absorbs money that could fund development.
The colonial legacy: economies were set up to export raw materials, and that pattern persists.

Tariff escalation: rich countries charge higher tariffs (taxes on imports) on processed goods than on raw materials, so processing at home does not pay; coffee beans enter rich markets with low tariffs, while roasted coffee faces higher ones.
notes.tip: Each reason needs developing with a short explanation, not just a name. Competition from established Asian manufacturers (which already have supply chains and skilled workers) and climate hazards such as drought (which reduce farm output and disrupt production) are two more reasons.

notes.b: Several measures try to help excluded regions join world trade and industry. They target debt, trade barriers and infrastructure.
points: The Heavily Indebted Poor Countries (HIPC) initiative, begun in 1996, gives debt relief (cancelling or reducing debts) through the World Bank and IMF.
The African Continental Free Trade Area, which removes trade barriers between African countries, began trading on 1 January 2021.
Chinese and other foreign investment is building infrastructure.
Fair trade (a system that pays producers a fairer price). There is more on this in 'Patterns in world trade'.

notes.b: Globalisation is the growing integration of the world's economies through trade, investment, MNCs, technology and the movement of people and ideas. It has changed what is traded, who trades and how goods move.
points: About 80% of world trade is linked to the international production networks of MNCs (UNCTAD, 2013).
Much of it is intra-firm trade, between parts of the same company or with its suppliers in global value chains (production split into stages across countries).
Trade is increasingly in components rather than finished goods, because each stage of production crosses borders.
Trade in services and digital trade has grown rapidly.
New trading powers, led by China, have entered world trade.
The WTO (World Trade Organization) and trade blocs have lowered barriers, so goods cross borders more easily.
Containerisation (shipping goods in standard steel boxes) and huge ports have cut the cost of shipping, so distant trade pays.
E-commerce (online selling) brings small sellers into world markets, so they can reach buyers abroad.
notes.tip: A short question may ask you to define globalisation. For how it changed world trade, give one point per effect.

notes.b: Globalisation does not benefit everyone equally. Some groups and regions gain, others lose.
points: Consumers gain cheaper goods, because production moves to low-cost countries.
NICs and China gain jobs and growth, because factories locate there.
Manufacturing regions in the core lose jobs, because production moves abroad.
Excluded regions fall further behind, because they get little of the new investment.
Workers in low-wage assembly can face poor and unsafe conditions, as the Rana Plaza collapse showed.
Transporting goods over long distances has environmental costs.
notes.tip: Do not present globalisation as wholly good or wholly bad; give both sides.

notes.b: Since 2018 some governments have pushed back against open trade, raising barriers between major economies.
points: The US-China trade war from 2018, the US tariffs of 2025 and Brexit have raised barriers between major economies.
Governments are reshoring strategic industries such as chips (the microchips in electronics), bringing production back home so they do not depend on distant suppliers.
Supply-chain worries grew after COVID-19.

notes.b: India's economy was tightly controlled before 1991, and it opened to globalisation only after a crisis.
points: Five-year plans from 1951 directed investment and production, so the state, not the market, decided what was made.
Protection (tariffs and rules that shut out imports) shielded Indian industries from foreign competition.
The Licence Raj: firms needed government licences to produce and expand, which limited competition and growth.
A balance-of-payments crisis (when a country cannot pay for its imports and debts) in 1991 forced change.
Prime Minister P. V. Narasimha Rao and Finance Minister Manmohan Singh removed most licences, cut tariffs and opened India to foreign investment.
notes.tip: The Higher Level 30-mark question asks you to explain the impact of globalisation on one developing economy. Use India's globalisation story only, with named examples and dates, and cover both positive and negative impacts.

notes.b: Globalisation brought rapid growth, new industries and foreign investment.
points: Bengaluru became known as the 'Silicon Valley of India'.

IT and business-process outsourcing (hiring firms abroad to run tasks such as customer service) grew rapidly; Tata Consultancy Services (founded 1968), Infosys (founded 1981) and Wipro grew, with Bengaluru as a major hub.
Texas Instruments opened a design centre in Bengaluru in 1985.
Maruti Suzuki, a joint venture (a company shared between partners) with Suzuki of Japan, made its first car in 1983.
India is a leading maker of generic medicines (cheaper copies of branded drugs), earning it the name 'pharmacy of the world'.
Make in India, launched in 2014, aimed to attract manufacturing; iPhones are assembled near Chennai and Bengaluru.
Services produce over half of India's GDP (the value of everything it produces), and India is among the world's five largest economies (early 2020s). A growing middle class has emerged.
Hundreds of millions of people have been moved out of extreme poverty, as growth created jobs and income.
notes.tip: Do not copy invented growth rates, job counts or poverty percentages from model answers; there is no checked figure for them.

notes.b: The gains from globalisation have been uneven, and it has brought costs for some people and places.
points: Inequality exists between cities and rural areas, and between states.
Small farmers are exposed to world prices, so they can lose when prices fall.
Farmers' protests in 2020-21 were against three farm laws, which were repealed in November 2021.
Most workers are still in the informal sector (jobs without contracts, regular pay or legal protection).
Pollution and accidents at MNC plants: the Bhopal gas leak at the Union Carbide pesticide plant in December 1984 killed thousands; Union Carbide was a US MNC.
notes.tip: Give no exact Bhopal death toll. Balance the answer with the positive impacts.

notes.b: China is a second developing economy, which opened to the world after 1978. It gained enormous growth but also costs.
points: Reforms under Deng Xiaoping from 1978 opened China to foreign trade and investment.
Special Economic Zones from 1980 attracted foreign investment, such as Shenzhen.
China joined the WTO on 11 December 2001, which gave it easier access to world markets.
China has been the largest goods exporter since 2009.
About 800 million people have been lifted out of extreme poverty since 1978 (World Bank).
Inequality exists between the coast and the interior, because growth centred on coastal zones.
Pollution from rapid industrial growth and dependence on exports are costs of this model, because a fall in world demand would hit China's economy.

notes.b: Bangladesh shows both sides of globalisation: jobs from the garment industry, and the dangers of low-cost production.
points: Ready-made garments are most of Bangladesh's exports; it is the world's second-largest garment exporter after China.
The garment industry provides jobs, especially for women.
Rana Plaza, Savar, near Dhaka, collapsed on 24 April 2013, killing over 1,100 garment workers. It was a building collapse, not a fire.
The Accord on Fire and Building Safety in Bangladesh, signed in 2013 by clothing brands and unions, introduced factory inspections.
notes.tip: The Rana Plaza toll is 'over 1,100'; do not give a different figure. It was a building collapse, not a fire.

keyTerms.definition: A factory carrying out one stage of production, such as processing a raw material, making a component or assembling a product.
An area where firms import components and export finished goods free of customs duty, with tax breaks.
An assembly plant along Mexico's border with the USA that imports components duty-free and exports finished goods to the USA.
A wealthy, densely developed area with capital, MNC headquarters, research and development, and political power.
A poorer area that supplies raw materials, food and cheap labour, with weak infrastructure and out-migration.
Newly industrialised countries moving from the periphery towards the core.
The process by which success attracts more investment, people and services, which increases success further.
The draining of capital and skilled people from a periphery to a core.
A simple North–South division between the rich north and the poor south, proposed in the Brandt Report of 1980.
Higher tariffs on processed goods than on raw materials, which discourages processing in the exporting country.
Moving production back to the home country from abroad.
The growing integration of the world's economies through trade, investment, MNCs, technology and the movement of people and ideas.

factCards.term: Why basic processing units are spread across many countries
factCards.definition: Cheap labour for labour-intensive assembly; nearness to raw materials or markets; getting inside trade blocs; tax breaks, grants and export processing zones; falling transport and communication costs; spreading risk, so one disaster or strike cannot stop all production.

factCards.term: Nike: how a manufacturer without factories spreads production
factCards.definition: Founded as Blue Ribbon Sports (1964) by Phil Knight and Bill Bowerman; renamed Nike in 1971. Design and marketing stay in Beaverton, Oregon; contract factories in Vietnam (the largest), China and Indonesia make its shoes. 1990s sweatshop criticism led to factory monitoring.

factCards.term: Export processing zones: three named examples with dates
factCards.definition: Shannon Free Zone, Co. Clare (1959), one of the world's first; Shenzhen, China, a Special Economic Zone from 1980 (over 17 million people by 2020); maquiladoras along Mexico's border with the USA, such as at Tijuana and Ciudad Juárez, from 1965.

factCards.term: Disadvantages of a spread-out production system
factCards.definition: Long supply chains are easily disrupted (2021 chip shortage, Ever Given, Red Sea attacks); branch plants close when costs change; some plants pay low wages with poor conditions; long-distance transport harms the environment. Responses: reshoring and friend-shoring.

factCards.term: How the global core developed
factCards.definition: Britain industrialised first (late 18th century), then western Europe and the USA; colonies supplied raw materials and markets, and profits were reinvested at home; cumulative causation (Myrdal, 1957) drew in more investment and people; backwash drained the periphery.

factCards.term: How the global periphery developed, or failed to
factCards.definition: Colonial economies were built to export one or two raw materials; railways ran from mines and plantations to ports, not between regions; colonisers drew the borders; after independence, falling commodity prices, debt and conflict held them back.

factCards.term: Global core, semi-periphery and periphery: named examples
factCards.definition: Core: the USA, western Europe's Blue Banana and Japan. Semi-periphery: South Korea earlier; China, India, Brazil and Mexico now. Periphery: most of sub-Saharan Africa, parts of Latin America and South Asia. Ireland became core-like through MNC investment.

factCards.term: Sub-Saharan Africa: evidence of exclusion from world manufacturing
factCards.definition: Mostly unprocessed raw-material exports: Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana grow over half the world's cocoa, mostly sold as beans; oil is most of Nigeria's exports and copper most of Zambia's; the Democratic Republic of the Congo mines most of the world's cobalt but exports it raw.

factCards.term: Why sub-Saharan Africa is excluded: infrastructure and physical reasons
factCards.definition: Poor roads and ports and unreliable electricity; 16 landlocked countries, such as Chad, Niger, Mali and South Sudan, facing high transport costs to reach ports; climate hazards such as drought disrupting farming and production.

factCards.term: Why sub-Saharan Africa is excluded: political and human reasons
factCards.definition: Political instability, conflict and corruption scare off investors; low levels of education and skills, and poor health, limit the workforce; small, poor home markets give firms little reason to produce locally; heavy debt absorbs money for development.

factCards.term: Why sub-Saharan Africa is excluded: trade and historical reasons
factCards.definition: A colonial legacy of economies built to export raw materials; tariff escalation, as coffee beans enter rich markets at low tariffs while roasted coffee faces higher ones, so processing at home does not pay; competition from established Asian manufacturers.

factCards.term: Sudan: a named example of a country excluded from manufacturing
factCards.definition: Civil war between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces since April 2023 has caused one of the world's largest displacement crises. South Sudan's independence in 2011 took most of the oil fields, Sudan's main export base.

factCards.term: Attempts to reduce Africa's exclusion from world trade
factCards.definition: Debt relief through the Heavily Indebted Poor Countries initiative (World Bank and IMF, 1996); the African Continental Free Trade Area, trading from 1 January 2021; Chinese and other foreign investment in infrastructure; fair trade.

factCards.term: Globalisation's effects on world trade: give seven
factCards.definition: About 80% of world trade is linked to MNC production networks (UNCTAD, 2013), much of it intra-firm; more trade in components; fast-growing services and digital trade; new powers led by China; lower barriers (WTO, trade blocs); containerisation; e-commerce.

factCards.term: Globalisation: winners and losers
factCards.definition: Winners: consumers (cheaper goods); NICs and China (jobs and growth). Losers: core manufacturing regions (lost jobs); excluded regions (falling further behind); low-wage assembly workers in unsafe conditions (Rana Plaza). Transport also adds environmental costs.

factCards.term: Reaction against globalisation: recent examples
factCards.definition: The US–China trade war (from 2018), US tariffs (2025) and Brexit raised barriers between major economies; governments are reshoring strategic industries such as chips; supply-chain worries grew after COVID-19.

factCards.term: India before 1991, and the 1991 reforms
factCards.definition: Five-year plans (from 1951), protection and the Licence Raj (permits to produce or expand) held back growth. After a 1991 balance-of-payments crisis, P. V. Narasimha Rao and Manmohan Singh removed most licences, cut tariffs and opened India to foreign investment.

factCards.term: India: positive impacts of globalisation on IT and services
factCards.definition: Bengaluru became the 'Silicon Valley of India'; IT and business-process outsourcing grew, led by Tata Consultancy Services (1968), Infosys (1981) and Wipro; Texas Instruments opened a Bengaluru design centre in 1985. Services now give over half of India's GDP.

factCards.term: India: positive impacts of globalisation on industry and living standards
factCards.definition: Maruti Suzuki, a joint venture with Japan's Suzuki, made its first car in 1983; India is the 'pharmacy of the world' for generic medicines; Make in India (2014) and iPhone assembly near Chennai; a growing middle class; hundreds of millions lifted out of extreme poverty.

factCards.term: India: negative impacts of globalisation
factCards.definition: Inequality between cities and rural areas and between states; small farmers exposed to world prices (2020–21 protests against three farm laws, repealed November 2021); most workers still informal; MNC accidents such as the Bhopal gas leak at Union Carbide's plant (1984).

factCards.term: China since 1978: positive and negative impacts of globalisation
factCards.definition: Reforms from 1978, SEZs from 1980 and WTO entry (2001) made China the largest goods exporter (since 2009) and lifted about 800 million people out of extreme poverty (World Bank). Costs: inequality between coast and interior, pollution, dependence on exports.

factCards.term: Bangladesh: garment exports, Rana Plaza and the Accord
factCards.definition: Garments are most of its exports; it is the world's second-largest garment exporter after China, with jobs especially for women. On 24 April 2013 Rana Plaza at Savar, near Dhaka, collapsed, killing over 1,100 garment workers; the 2013 Accord on Fire and Building Safety brought factory inspections.

questions.prompt: Explain the impact of globalisation on one developing economy that you have studied.
questions.model: India is the developing economy studied here. Before 1991 its economy was tightly controlled: five-year plans from 1951 directed investment, protection shielded Indian industries from foreign competition, and the Licence Raj required firms to hold government licences to produce and expand. A balance-of-payments crisis in 1991 forced change. Prime Minister P. V. Narasimha Rao and Finance Minister Manmohan Singh then removed most licences, cut tariffs and opened India to foreign investment. The positive impacts were rapid growth in IT and business-process outsourcing. Bengaluru, known as the Silicon Valley of India, became a hub for firms such as Tata Consultancy Services (founded 1968), Infosys (founded 1981) and Wipro, and Texas Instruments opened a design centre there in 1985. Foreign investment brought Maruti Suzuki, a joint venture with Suzuki of Japan, which made its first car in 1983. India became a leading maker of generic medicines and exports cars and pharmaceuticals. Make in India, launched in 2014, aimed to attract manufacturing, and iPhones are now assembled near Chennai and Bengaluru. Services produce over half of India's GDP, a growing middle class has emerged, and hundreds of millions of people have been moved out of extreme poverty. The negative impacts were serious too. Inequality exists between cities and rural areas and between states. Small farmers are exposed to world prices, which led to the farmers' protests of 2020–21 against three farm laws, repealed in November 2021. Most workers remain in the informal sector without security. Pollution and MNC accidents also occurred, as in the Bhopal gas leak at the Union Carbide pesticide plant in December 1984, which killed thousands. Overall, globalisation has brought growth and poverty reduction to India alongside inequality, insecure work and environmental harm.

questions.prompt: Examine why some regions of the world are excluded from world manufacturing activity.
questions.model: Sub-Saharan Africa is the main excluded region. It has a very small share of world manufacturing and exports mostly unprocessed raw materials: crude oil from Nigeria, copper from Zambia and cobalt from the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Poor infrastructure, including roads, ports and unreliable electricity, raises the cost of producing and moving goods. Africa has 16 landlocked countries, such as Chad, Niger, Mali and South Sudan, which face high transport costs to reach ports. Political instability, conflict and corruption scare off investment; the civil war in Sudan since April 2023 is one example, and it has caused one of the world's largest displacement crises. Low levels of education, skills and health limit the workforce, and small, poor home markets give firms little reason to produce locally. Heavy debt absorbs money that could fund development. Tariff escalation means rich countries charge higher tariffs on processed goods than on raw materials: coffee beans enter rich markets with low tariffs, while roasted coffee faces higher ones, so processing at home does not pay. The colonial legacy left economies built around exporting raw materials, a pattern that persists. Competition from established Asian manufacturers, which already have supply chains and skilled workers, makes entry harder. Climate hazards such as drought reduce farm output. Responses include debt relief through the HIPC initiative from 1996, the African Continental Free Trade Area, which began trading on 1 January 2021, and foreign investment in infrastructure. Together these barriers explain why the region remains largely excluded from world manufacturing.

questions.prompt: Examine how globalisation has affected world trade.
questions.model: Globalisation is the growing integration of the world's economies through trade, investment, multinational companies (MNCs), technology and the movement of people and ideas. World trade has grown faster than output, and about 80% of it is linked to the international production networks of MNCs (UNCTAD, 2013). Much of it is intra-firm trade, between parts of the same company or with its suppliers in global value chains. Basic processing units are spread across countries: Nike designs and sells shoes from Beaverton, Oregon, while independent contract factories in Vietnam, China and Indonesia make them, and export processing zones such as Shannon Free Zone and the Shenzhen Special Economic Zone, as well as Mexico's maquiladoras, allow duty-free assembly for export. Trade is increasingly in components rather than finished goods, and trade in services and digital trade has grown rapidly. New trading powers, led by China, have entered world trade, and China has been the largest goods exporter since 2009. The WTO and trade blocs have lowered barriers, while containerisation and huge ports have cut shipping costs, and e-commerce brings small sellers into world markets. These changes have created winners and losers. Consumers gain cheaper goods, and NICs and China gain jobs and growth. Manufacturing regions in the core lose jobs, excluded regions fall further behind, and workers in low-wage assembly can face poor and unsafe conditions, as the Rana Plaza collapse of 2013 showed. Transport over long distances has environmental costs. In reaction, the US–China trade war from 2018, the US tariffs of 2025 and Brexit have raised barriers, and governments are reshoring strategic industries such as chips. Supply-chain worries grew after COVID-19. Globalisation has therefore increased world trade and linked economies closely, although much of that trade is controlled by MNCs and some regions have been left behind.
